It is rare in the New Testament, occurring just twice in the Byzantine text and only once in the critical text (Acts 2:11), where it describes the "wonderful works of God." An interesting detail from the papyri is that μεγαλεῖον became a ceremonial title of honor—"his highness" or "your magnificence"—used for Caesar and even officials like a Prefect.

prose.article: This word points to overwhelming greatness and splendor, the kind of grandeur that inspires awe. prose.article: μεγαλύνω covers two related ideas: literally making something bigger (like enlarging the borders of garments in Matthew 23:5) and figuratively praising or exalting someone as great (as when Mary's soul "magnifies" the Lord). prose.article: μέγας is the all-purpose word for "big" in the broadest sense, covering physical size, intensity, loudness, and rank or importance. Of its 240 New Testament occurrences, 58% are rendered "great" and another 19% "loud" (as in a loud voice or cry), with the rest expressing comparison—"greater," "greater than," or "greatest." In the Septuagint it overwhelmingly translates Hebrew גָּדוֹל ("great," 396×). Its meaning is so tied to surrounding verbs that in 78 of its 111 New Testament occurrences it gets absorbed into the phrasing and has no separate English word of its own; when it does surface, translators render it "about" (14×), "going" (10×), or "come" (6×). Everyday Koine papyri confirm this ordinary usage, as in a 2nd-century BC letter saying "I am about to import in the month of Mesore."
prose.caution: Because the word so often blends into the verb it modifies — and the Septuagint Hebrew matches are sparse and inconsistent — its precise force in any verse depends heavily on context.

prose.def: A limb or part of the body, used literally of physical body parts and figuratively of individuals as parts of a unified body such as Christ's church.
prose.article: μέλος refers to a part or limb of the body, and Bible translators render it as "part" in about 43% of its 34 New Testament occurrences and as some form of "member" or "body" in most of the rest. The word stretches naturally from literal anatomy to a figurative sense in which believers are described as members of one another or of Christ's body. Everyday Koine confirms the basic meaning vividly: a papyrus from around A.D. 131 complains of being beaten "on every limb of my body" (μέλος τοῦ σώματος). In the Septuagint it most often translates the Hebrew נֵתַח, a word for a piece or cut portion of an animal.

prose.def: Melchizedek, the indeclinable proper name for the priest-king of Salem, used in Hebrews both as a personal referent and as a type defining Christ's priestly order.
prose.article: Μελχισεδέκ is simply the Greek spelling of the Hebrew name Malki-tsedek, the priest-king of Salem, and it never changes form (it's indeclinable). All 9 New Testament occurrences sit in Hebrews, where the rendering splits between naming the man himself (3×) and the recurring phrase "the order of Melchizedek" describing a priesthood (5×). One nice detail from the papyri evidence: the name is never spelled in Greek with a ζ in either Testament, and Hebrews famously describes him as "without father, without mother" (Heb 7:8).
prose.caution: This is a proper name confined to Hebrews, so its meaning is tied entirely to that book's argument rather than a flexible word range.

prose.def: To be a matter of care or concern to someone, used almost always impersonally (it matters, it concerns) with a dative of person and various object constructions.
senseLabels: care / concern (impersonal, with dative of person)
prose.article: This verb almost always shows up in the impersonal form "it matters" or "it concerns," usually paired with a person in the dative — as in "do you not care that we are perishing?" The Majority Standard Bible renders it as "care" in 4 of its 9 occurrences (80% of the times it gets its own English word), while the other 4 are absorbed into phrasing with no separate word. A nice everyday parallel survives in the papyri: a private letter from A.D. 84 reads "I know that you are concerned about me," using this very verb the same way the New Testament does.
prose.caution: Classical lexica note a transitive sense "to care for," but Abbott-Smith says it appears in neither the Septuagint nor the New Testament, so the biblical range is narrower than the dictionaries' full entry suggests.

prose.def: Parchments: sheets or rolls made from prepared animal skin used as a writing surface, possibly for scriptures or personal notes.
senseLabels: a sheet or roll of parchment
prose.article: This word names parchment, the durable writing material made from animal skin. It's actually a Greek spelling of the Latin word membrana, and Moulton-Milligan note it shows up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions. In the New Testament it appears only once, in 2 Timothy 4:13, where Paul asks Timothy to bring his parchments—likely scrolls of the Old Testament Scriptures.
prose.caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its range cannot be measured from biblical usage alone.
